title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 65–66
description: Colour shades and figurative colour language; nuanced vocabulary for rapid, uncontrolled, gradual and changing movement.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study using the user-provided book. Vocabulary selections reflect the source teaching pages and selected exercise/answer-key targets, while translations, explanations and example sentences are newly written; no original exercises or extended passages are reproduced.

audit.scope: Both teaching pages and exercises for Units 65 and 66, including colour charts, metaphors, usage restrictions, speed contrasts and corresponding answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA for selected short lexical items only where confidently established; blank IPA for longer expressions and uncertain pronunciations. Connected-speech detail and accents are not exhaustively represented.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing fields are in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared all four source pages and the corresponding answer key; checked semantic nuance, collocations, usage restrictions, register and provenance; independently authored examples; checked JSON structure, IDs, types and word-audio targets with a local script.
audit.limitations: Static validation only. No live VocabLab import, browser TTS or pronunciation-recognition test was performed. No bundled MP3 files are included.

units.title: Unit 65 — All the colours of the rainbow
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 136–137 (PDF pages 138–139).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
learningObjectives: Distinguish intense, pastel, vivid, harsh and approximate colour descriptions and their typical collocations.
Use gemstone-based colour vocabulary and suffixes such as -ish with attention to natural context.
Interpret colour-based idioms, professional labels and evaluative metaphors, including exercise-only contrasts.
Avoid confusing literal colour with expressions about danger, emotion, reputation, money and the environment.

sectionsChecked: A, B and C teaching sections, charts, lexical and metaphorical usage
All exercises and corresponding answer-key entries

items.example: The village was pitch black after the power failed.
items.note: An especially intense black, normally describing darkness rather than hair.

items.example: Her jet black hair stood out against the pale scarf.
items.note: An intense black, particularly natural for hair or eyes; contrasts with pitch black darkness.

items.example: A scarlet ribbon marked the entrance to the exhibition.
items.note: A conspicuously bright red rather than a dark red.

items.example: The evening sky turned crimson above the coastline.
items.note: A strong, deep red, usually less bright than scarlet.

items.example: The designer chose a shocking pink jacket for the final look.
items.note: An extremely vivid shade of pink; often deliberately eye-catching.

items.example: The ginger cat was sleeping beside the fireplace.
items.note: As a colour adjective, normally describes hair or animal fur.

items.example: He wore a navy suit to the award ceremony.
items.note: A very dark blue, especially used for clothes; navy eyes is not a normal collocation.

items.example: The shallows appeared turquoise in the afternoon sunlight.
items.note: Greenish-blue, typical of sea water, textiles and paint, but unusual for eye colour.

items.example: A lime scarf added a bright contrast to her dark coat.
items.note: As a colour word, a vivid yellowish green; not the fruit itself.

items.example: The office was decorated in understated beige tones.
items.note: A pale creamy-brown colour associated with neutral palettes.

items.example: He described his own hair as a rather mousy brown.
items.note: Describes an unremarkable light-brown shade of hair, often with a negative nuance.

items.example: The rider led a chestnut horse into the arena.
items.note: A rich reddish-brown shade used especially for horses and hair.

items.example: Her auburn curls caught the light as she turned.
items.note: A reddish-brown colour most commonly associated with hair.

items.example: The artist highlighted the dress with ruby accents.
items.note: When describing colour, suggests a deep, jewel-like red; also names a precious stone.

items.example: An emerald silk blouse was displayed in the shop window.
items.note: A bright, rich green colour named after the gemstone.

items.example: Amber light filtered through the old glass.
items.note: A warm orange-yellow shade; also the name of fossilised tree resin.

items.example: They repainted the dining room in a soft coral shade.
items.note: A pinkish-orange colour, not identical to ruby red.

items.example: The fabric had a rich sapphire finish.
items.note: As a colour term, a deep blue derived from the gemstone name.

items.example: She selected jade tiles for the bathroom walls.
items.note: A green gemstone name also used as a colour adjective.

items.example: The art teacher used primary colours to demonstrate colour mixing.
items.note: In the book’s traditional painting context, these are red, blue and yellow; light uses a different primary-colour model.

items.example: Pastel colours made the small room feel brighter and calmer.
items.note: Pale, soft shades rather than saturated, intense colours.

items.example: Mauve flowers grew beside the path.
items.note: A relatively pale purple shade, used as a pastel-colour example.

items.example: The posters used strong colours to attract attention.
items.note: Vivid or saturated colours, presented as the opposite of pastel shades.

items.example: The harsh colours of the advert were uncomfortable to look at.
items.note: Harsh conveys disapproval of an unpleasantly strong combination, unlike vivid.

items.example: The photographs captured the vivid colours of the street festival.
items.note: Strong, clear and bright; normally complimentary or neutral, unlike harsh.

items.example: The runners wore fluorescent colours to remain visible at dusk.
items.note: Very bright colours that appear to glow; not necessarily literally self-luminous.

items.example: An electric blue sign dominated the shopfront.
items.note: An exceptionally bright, striking blue; electric is not normally applied to black.

items.example: The graphic designer used electric green for the call-to-action text.
items.note: An exceptionally intense green, not simply an ordinary dark green.

items.pt: um leve tom de; um toque de
items.example: The white paint had a tinge of blue under artificial lighting.
items.note: A tinge of + colour describes a very slight trace of a colour, rather than a fully coloured surface.

items.example: The artist presented a monochrome series of photographs.
items.note: Using one colour or tones of one colour; can include black, white and greys.

items.example: A bluish mist settled over the hills before sunrise.
items.note: The suffix -ish signals an approximate colour rather than a pure shade.

items.example: A reddish stain appeared on the wooden table.
items.note: The suffix -ish indicates a colour that is partly red, not an exact red.

items.example: The seawater looked bluey green from the cliff.
items.note: The informal -y ending can indicate that another hue is partly present; spelling varies.

items.example: After weeks of grey weather, she began to feel blue.
items.note: Informal expression for sadness rather than literal skin colour.

items.example: The policy could have a substantial impact on blue-collar workers.
items.note: Refers broadly to manual or industrial occupations, not the colour of clothing.

items.pt: ficar furioso; perder a cabeça de raiva
items.example: He saw red when he discovered the forged figures.
items.note: Informal idiom meaning suddenly become extremely angry.

items.example: The security team declared a red alert following the breach.
items.note: A warning indicating an especially high level of danger.

items.pt: sinal de alerta; indício de problema
items.example: The unexplained discrepancy was a red flag for the auditors.
items.note: A warning sign that something may be wrong, dangerous or deceptive.

items.example: The visiting researchers received red-carpet treatment from their hosts.
items.note: Exceptionally welcoming, prestigious or attentive treatment.

items.example: The laboratory inauguration was a red-letter day for the institute.
items.note: A particularly significant or happy date, not a day written in red ink.

items.pt: de esquerda radical; comunista (em certos contextos políticos)
items.example: The historian explained why red was associated with revolutionary movements.
items.note: In political history, red can mean communist or strongly left-wing; its implications depend on time and context.

items.pt: parecer enjoado; estar com aparência de náusea
items.example: He looked green after the rough ferry crossing.
items.note: Can suggest nausea or seasickness rather than an actual green complexion.

items.pt: verde de inveja; morrendo de inveja
items.example: She was green with envy when her rival won the scholarship.
items.note: A fixed expression meaning extremely envious.

items.example: The island invested in green tourism to protect its coastline.
items.note: Green here conveys environmental concern, not a literal colour.

items.example: The Green Party highlighted the environmental impact of the proposal.
items.note: A common political party name associated with environmental protection; national parties differ.

items.example: Without additional funding, the project faced a black future.
items.note: Black can convey despair or lack of hope; a strongly negative metaphor.

items.pt: com cara de poucos amigos; visivelmente furioso
items.example: The director looked as black as thunder when the deadline was missed.
items.note: A British expression meaning visibly furious or in a very bad mood.

items.example: The scarce medicine was being sold on the black market.
items.note: Illegal or unauthorised trading, not merely a market with dark stalls.

items.example: He was labelled the black sheep of the family for rejecting their traditions.
items.note: A family member perceived as different or disapproved of; often carries judgement.

items.example: Repeated late submissions put a black mark against his record.
items.note: A negative judgement or mark against somebody’s reputation or performance.

items.example: The rules leave a grey area concerning data ownership.
items.note: A situation without a clear classification or legal or moral boundary.

items.example: Solving the puzzle required a bit of grey matter.
items.note: Literal brain tissue, also used figuratively for intelligence.

items.example: The detective urged the team to use their grey cells.
items.note: Informal metaphor for mental effort or intelligence.

items.pt: branco como a neve; extremamente puro
items.example: The freshly painted wall was white as snow.
items.note: Can describe literal whiteness; white also suggests innocence in colour metaphors.

items.pt: acima de qualquer suspeita; de reputação impecável
items.example: The candidate presented herself as whiter than white despite the allegations.
items.note: Often used ironically of supposedly impeccable conduct or reputation.

items.pt: pálido como um fantasma; muito pálido
items.example: He went white as a sheet when the results were announced.
items.note: Conveys sudden pallor caused by fright or shock.

items.pt: experiência de tirar o fôlego; passeio assustador
items.example: The final descent made the roller coaster a white-knuckle ride.
items.note: An intensely frightening or thrilling ride; metaphorical in other contexts.

items.example: The survey compared commuting habits among white-collar workers.
items.note: Refers broadly to office and professional occupations, not white uniforms.

items.example: He has had the blues ever since his closest friend moved abroad.
items.note: Informal expression describing sadness; more sustained than a momentary disappointment.

items.pt: difamar alguém; manchar a reputação de alguém
items.example: The false allegations were intended to blacken her name.
items.note: To harm a person’s reputation by speaking badly of them; not literal colouring.

items.example: The archive contains thousands of black and white photographs.
items.note: Fixed word order in the familiar phrase: black and white, not white and black.

items.example: The company finished the financial year in the black.
items.note: An accounting expression for positive balance or profitability, opposite of in the red.

items.example: The department remained in the red after unexpected costs.
items.note: An accounting expression for a negative balance or debt.

items.example: She told a white lie to avoid spoiling the surprise.
items.note: A minor, usually socially motivated untruth; not necessarily ethically harmless.

items.pt: pista falsa; informação que desvia a atenção
items.example: The apparent security flaw turned out to be a red herring.
items.note: Something that distracts attention from the real issue.

items.example: An offer of collaboration arrived out of the blue.
items.note: Something that happens without warning or expectation.

items.word: a red rag to a bull
items.example: Mentioning the cancelled contract was like a red rag to a bull.
items.note: British idiom for a topic or action that predictably provokes someone.

items.pt: talento para jardinagem; mão boa para plantas
items.example: Her green fingers have transformed the neglected courtyard.
items.note: British English idiom for a natural talent for growing plants.

items.pt: cinturão verde; zona de proteção ambiental urbana
items.example: The council restricted new housing on land designated as green belt.
items.note: In UK planning, protected open land around urban areas; rules vary by jurisdiction.

items.pt: documento de consulta pública para políticas governamentais
items.example: The ministry issued a green paper to invite public discussion of the reform.
items.note: In the UK, an initial consultation document, not an environmental policy by definition.

items.example: The retailer sells white goods such as fridges and washing machines.
items.note: A commercial category of major domestic appliances, regardless of colour.

items.pt: roxo de frio; muito afetado pelo frio
items.example: The hikers were blue with cold when they reached the shelter.
items.note: Suggests severe cold or a bluish appearance, often hyperbolically.

items.pt: de sangue azul; de origem aristocrática
items.example: He liked to boast that his ancestors were blue-blooded.
items.note: Describes aristocratic lineage, sometimes used critically or humorously.

units.title: Unit 66 — Speed: fast and slow
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 138–139 (PDF pages 140–141).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
learningObjectives: Distinguish rapid motion, sudden escape, uncontrolled movement and small hurried steps.
Choose context-sensitive verbs for dramatic increases, sharp declines and gradual changes.
Contrast figurative and literal uses of soar, plummet, career, bolt and creep.
Use natural collocations, verb patterns and register for describing how people, vehicles and prices move.

sectionsChecked: A, B and C teaching sections, examples and contextual usage
All exercises and corresponding answer-key entries

items.example: She dashed across campus to retrieve the forgotten presentation.
items.note: Moving or going very quickly, often because time is short.

items.example: He came flying down the stairs when he heard the alarm.
items.note: Figuratively describes very rapid motion, not necessarily literal flight.

items.pt: correr às pressas; disparar em direção a algo
items.example: The technicians raced to the control room when the warning appeared.
items.note: To move very quickly, often towards a destination or under pressure.

items.pt: disparar; sair correndo ou em alta velocidade
items.example: The motorbike tore down the empty road.
items.note: As a motion verb, pronounced /teə/ in British English and often followed by a direction.

items.pt: dar uma passada rápida; ir rapidinho
items.example: I will nip to the post office before the meeting.
items.note: Mainly British informal English for making a quick short trip.

items.example: Could you pop into the pharmacy on your way home?
items.note: Informal for a brief visit or short trip, often in pop into or pop over.

items.pt: mover-se num movimento rápido e repentino
items.example: A lizard darted beneath the rocks as we approached.
items.note: Sudden brief movement, common for animals or people avoiding notice.

items.example: A delivery scooter zipped past the traffic queue.
items.note: Informal for moving quickly, particularly vehicles and small moving objects.

items.example: The express train whizzed through the station.
items.note: Suggests rapid motion, sometimes with a whirring sound; British spelling whizz.

items.example: The frightened horse bolted through the open gate.
items.note: Rapid escape from danger or alarm, rather than simply travelling quickly.

items.example: The van careered across the wet road before hitting a barrier.
items.note: British English verb meaning move fast and out of control, not pursue a profession.

items.pt: correr com passinhos rápidos; sair correndo
items.example: The puppies scampered across the grass towards their owner.
items.note: Light, quick steps, especially by small animals or children.

items.example: Staff scurried between rooms as the conference began.
items.note: Rapid small steps, often with a sense of nervous urgency.

items.pt: sair correndo rapidamente com passinhos; escapulir
items.example: Several crabs scuttled between the stones.
items.note: Quick, short-legged movement, particularly by small creatures.

items.example: We need to speed up the review process to meet the deadline.
items.note: Applies to people, vehicles and processes; a separable phrasal verb when transitive.

items.example: The train accelerated after leaving the platform.
items.note: Primarily vehicles in literal movement, but also growth and other processes figuratively.

items.pt: caminhar rapidamente para problemas graves; precipitar-se rumo a dificuldades
items.example: Without effective oversight, the organisation could career into serious trouble.
items.note: Figurative extension of career: rapid movement towards a bad outcome with little control.

items.example: The rescue worker plunged into the river to reach the swimmer.
items.note: Abrupt downward movement literally, or a sudden decline in figures or conditions.

items.example: Investor confidence plummeted after the unexpected announcement.
items.note: A particularly steep, sudden drop, common in figures and financial reporting.

items.pt: mergulhado em desespero; tomado pelo desespero
items.example: The unexpected loss left him plunged into despair for several weeks.
items.note: Be plunged into describes a sudden entry into an extreme emotional condition.

items.example: Rental prices rocketed in the city centre over the summer.
items.note: Rapid and dramatic upward change, especially prices and quantities.

items.example: Demand for renewable energy soared after the policy change.
items.note: Can refer to rising prices, quantities, birds or strong positive emotions.

items.example: Her spirits soared when the committee approved her proposal.
items.note: Figurative soar conveys elation or a sudden rise in happiness.

items.example: Sales slumped during the prolonged transport strike.
items.note: A pronounced downturn, particularly in markets, activity or performance.

items.example: The share price tumbled on news of the failed merger.
items.note: May describe a physical fall or a steep decline in prices.

items.example: Energy prices rocketed after the supply disruption.
items.note: A typical financial collocation for a fast, dramatic increase in prices.

items.example: Profits plummeted after the company lost its largest customer.
items.note: A typical reporting collocation for a sharp decrease in profit.

items.pt: andar a passos de tartaruga; rastejar
items.example: The traffic crawled along the ring road in the evening rush.
items.note: A very slow movement; also literal crawling on hands and knees.

items.example: She crept down the corridor to avoid waking the baby.
items.note: Quiet or cautious slow movement; past tense and participle crept.

items.example: Subscription fees have been creeping up since January.
items.note: Slow, gradual increases that may be hard to notice initially.

items.example: He tottered down the steps under the weight of two suitcases.
items.note: Unsteady motion, often with difficulty balancing, rather than deliberate delay.

items.pt: aproximar-se de lado; chegar discretamente a alguém
items.example: She sidled up to the manager to ask a delicate question.
items.note: Approach sideways or hesitantly, often to avoid drawing attention.

items.example: Stop dawdling outside the café or we will miss the train.
items.note: To move more slowly than necessary or waste time; often said critically.

items.pt: engolir a comida depressa; comer muito rápido
items.example: He bolted his food before rushing back to the laboratory.
items.note: Here bolt means eat too fast; this is different from bolting away to escape danger.

items.example: A traffic jam delayed the shuttle bus by nearly an hour.
items.note: In the exercise, crawling traffic is associated with a traffic jam.

items.example: She was in a hurry and left her notebook on the train.
items.note: A natural fixed phrase explaining urgent, rapid movement.
